title: Acts 27:1–26
context: Paul sails for Italy as a prisoner under a centurion named Julius, who treats him kindly. Contrary winds slow the voyage, and at Fair Havens Paul warns that continuing will bring loss, but the centurion follows the pilot and owner. A violent northeaster drives the ship for days until all hope of rescue is abandoned. Paul then stands up and tells them to take heart: an angel of God has assured him that he must stand before Caesar and that God has granted him the lives of all who sail with him, though they will run aground on an island.

verses.text: When it was determined that we should sail for Italy, they delivered Paul and certain other prisoners to a centurion named Julius, of the Augustan band.
verses.arminianNotes: Paul and other prisoners are handed over to Julius, a centurion of the Augustan Cohort. The “we” returns, so Luke is on board for the voyage.
verses.reformedNotes: Luke’s account of the voyage is so detailed that historians of ancient seafaring still use it.

verses.text: Embarking in a ship of Adramyttium, which was about to sail to places on the coast of Asia, we put to sea, Aristarchus, a Macedonian of Thessalonica being with us.
verses.arminianNotes: They embark on a ship from Adramyttium bound for ports along Asia, accompanied by Aristarchus, a Macedonian from Thessalonica.
verses.reformedNotes: Aristarchus had been seized in the Ephesian riot (19:29) and later appears as Paul’s fellow prisoner (Colossians 4:10).

verses.text: The next day, we touched at Sidon. Julius treated Paul kindly and gave him permission to go to his friends and refresh himself.
verses.arminianNotes: At Sidon Julius treats Paul kindly and lets him visit friends to receive care.
verses.reformedNotes: A Roman officer’s courtesy becomes one of the means by which Paul is sustained.

verses.text: Putting to sea from there, we sailed under the lee of Cyprus, because the winds were contrary.
verses.arminianNotes: Contrary winds force them to sail under the lee of Cyprus, on its sheltered side.
verses.reformedNotes: Late-summer westerlies made the passage slow, a detail any Mediterranean sailor would recognize.

verses.text: When we had sailed across the sea which is off Cilicia and Pamphylia, we came to Myra, a city of Lycia.
verses.arminianNotes: They cross the open sea off Cilicia and Pamphylia and land at Myra in Lycia.
verses.reformedNotes: Myra was a major port for the Egyptian grain fleet bound for Rome.

verses.text: There the centurion found a ship of Alexandria sailing for Italy, and he put us on board.
verses.arminianNotes: There Julius finds an Alexandrian grain ship sailing for Italy and puts them aboard.
verses.reformedNotes: Grain ships were vital to Rome’s food supply, large enough to carry the 276 people counted in verse 37.

verses.text: When we had sailed slowly many days, and had come with difficulty opposite Cnidus, the wind not allowing us further, we sailed under the lee of Crete, opposite Salmone.
verses.arminianNotes: They sail slowly for many days and reach Cnidus with difficulty, then run under the lee of Crete off Salmone.
verses.reformedNotes: The winds keep blocking their course, foreshadowing the storm to come.

verses.text: With difficulty sailing along it we came to a certain place called Fair Havens, near the city of Lasea.
verses.arminianNotes: Coasting with difficulty, they reach a place called Fair Havens near the town of Lasea.
verses.reformedNotes: Fair Havens was an exposed bay, not a good winter harbor, which sets up the decision that follows.

verses.text: When much time had passed and the voyage was now dangerous because the Fast had now already gone by, Paul admonished them
verses.arminianNotes: Much time has passed and sailing is now dangerous, since the Fast, the Day of Atonement, has already gone by. That placed them in late September or October, near the end of the sailing season.
verses.reformedNotes: Luke dates the voyage by the Jewish calendar, a reminder that Paul still marked Israel’s holy days.

verses.text: and said to them, “Sirs, I perceive that the voyage will be with injury and much loss, not only of the cargo and the ship, but also of our lives.”
verses.arminianNotes: Paul warns that the voyage will bring disaster and heavy loss, not only of cargo and ship but also of their lives. His advice comes from experience; he had already been shipwrecked three times (2 Corinthians 11:25).
verses.reformedNotes: This is Paul’s judgment, not yet a revelation. God’s later word in verse 22 will correct the forecast about lives.

verses.text: But the centurion gave more heed to the master and to the owner of the ship than to those things which were spoken by Paul.
verses.arminianNotes: The centurion trusts the pilot and the ship’s owner more than Paul.
verses.reformedNotes: Expert opinion and commercial interest outweigh the prisoner’s warning, a natural choice that turns out wrong.

verses.text: Because the haven was not suitable to winter in, the majority advised going to sea from there, if by any means they could reach Phoenix and winter there, which is a port of Crete, looking southwest and northwest.
verses.arminianNotes: Because Fair Havens is unsuitable for wintering, the majority decide to try for Phoenix, a Cretan harbor facing southwest and northwest.
verses.reformedNotes: A majority vote decides the course, and the story will show its limits.

verses.text: When the south wind blew softly, supposing that they had obtained their purpose, they weighed anchor and sailed along Crete, close to shore.
verses.arminianNotes: A gentle south wind seems to give them what they want, so they weigh anchor and sail close along Crete.
verses.reformedNotes: The fair breeze looks like confirmation. Luke shows how quickly circumstances can mislead.

verses.text: But before long, a stormy wind beat down from shore, which is called Euroclydon.
verses.arminianNotes: Soon a violent wind called the Euraquilo, a northeaster, rushes down from the island.
verses.reformedNotes: The name, a mix of Greek and Latin, is the sailors’ own term. Luke records the storm as they knew it.

verses.text: When the ship was caught and couldn’t face the wind, we gave way to it and were driven along.
verses.arminianNotes: The ship is caught and cannot head into the wind, so they give way and are driven along.
verses.reformedNotes: Human control ends here. From this point the narrative turns to how God will keep his word.

verses.text: Running under the lee of a small island called Clauda, we were able, with difficulty, to secure the boat.
verses.arminianNotes: Running under the lee of a small island called Cauda, they barely manage to secure the ship’s boat.
verses.reformedNotes: Luke’s “we” suggests he helped haul the dinghy aboard.

verses.text: After they had hoisted it up, they used cables to help reinforce the ship. Fearing that they would run aground on the Syrtis sand bars, they lowered the sea anchor, and so were driven along.
verses.arminianNotes: They pass cables under the hull to brace it and, fearing the Syrtis sandbars off Libya, lower the gear and let the ship drift.
verses.reformedNotes: Undergirding was standard emergency practice. The crew does everything sound seamanship requires.

verses.text: As we labored exceedingly with the storm, the next day they began to throw things overboard.
verses.arminianNotes: Violently storm-tossed, they begin throwing cargo overboard the next day.
verses.reformedNotes: The jettison echoes Jonah 1:5, another storm in which sailors lightened a ship.

verses.text: On the third day, they threw out the ship’s tackle with their own hands.
verses.arminianNotes: On the third day they throw out the ship’s tackle with their own hands.
verses.reformedNotes: Even passengers join in, giving up equipment needed to sail.

verses.text: When neither sun nor stars shone on us for many days, and no small storm pressed on us, all hope that we would be saved was now taken away.
verses.arminianNotes: With neither sun nor stars visible for many days and the storm still raging, all hope of being saved is finally abandoned.
verses.reformedNotes: Without celestial navigation they are lost as well as battered. Luke marks this as the low point before God’s word arrives.

verses.text: When they had been long without food, Paul stood up in the middle of them and said, “Sirs, you should have listened to me, and not have set sail from Crete and have gotten this injury and loss.
verses.arminianNotes: After long abstinence from food, Paul stands among them and reminds them they should have listened to him and not left Crete.
verses.reformedNotes: The rebuke is not gloating. It establishes that Paul’s word can be trusted before he delivers God’s promise.

verses.text: Now I exhort you to cheer up, for there will be no loss of life among you, but only of the ship.
verses.arminianNotes: He urges them to take heart, for no life will be lost, only the ship. This corrects his own earlier prediction in verse 10.
verses.reformedNotes: The difference between verse 10 and verse 22 is the difference between Paul’s judgment and God’s revelation.

verses.text: For there stood by me this night an angel, belonging to the God whose I am and whom I serve,
verses.arminianNotes: An angel of the God to whom he belongs and whom he serves stood by him that night.
verses.reformedNotes: Paul introduces God to pagan sailors through his own relationship: belonging comes before serving.

verses.text: saying, ‘Don’t be afraid, Paul. You must stand before Caesar. Behold, God has granted you all those who sail with you.’
verses.arminianNotes: The angel said, “Don’t be afraid, Paul. You must stand before Caesar. God has granted you all who sail with you.” Arminian interpreters often read “granted” as God answering Paul’s intercession, so the lives of others were given in response to prayer.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters see the “must” of 23:11 reaffirmed in the middle of the storm. God’s purpose for Paul guarantees the lives of everyone aboard.

verses.text: Therefore, sirs, cheer up! For I believe God, that it will be just as it has been spoken to me.
verses.arminianNotes: “So take heart, men, for I believe God that it will be just as I have been told.” Faith here is trust in a specific promise.
verses.reformedNotes: Paul’s confidence rests entirely on God’s word, not on any sign of improving weather.

verses.text: But we must run aground on a certain island.”
verses.arminianNotes: “But we must run aground on some island.” The promise includes the wreck, not an escape from it.
verses.reformedNotes: God’s plan includes loss of the ship and the hardship of the landing. Deliverance comes through the disaster, not around it.
